question: What is the JUnit 5 test execution lifecycle?
title: JUnit 5 Test Lifecycle | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: The JUnit 5 lifecycle per class is: **`@BeforeAll`** once → then for **each** test method: **`@BeforeEach`** → **`@Test`** → **`@AfterEach`** → finally **`@AfterAll`** once. By default JUnit creates a **fresh test instance per method** (PER_METHOD), which is why `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` must be `static`. This per-test reset is what keeps tests independent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the exact order and why fresh-instance-per-method enforces isolation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking one instance is reused across tests, or that @BeforeAll runs before each test
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect PER_METHOD default to test independence and to the static requirement on @BeforeAll

sections.title: The Execution Lifecycle
sections.content: JUnit 5 runs a predictable sequence around your tests. **`@BeforeAll`** runs **once** before any test in the class (static by default). Then, for **each** test method, JUnit: creates a **new instance** of the test class, runs all **`@BeforeEach`** methods, runs the **`@Test`**, then all **`@AfterEach`** methods. After every test has run, **`@AfterAll`** runs **once**. The default test-instance lifecycle is **PER_METHOD** — a fresh object per test — which guarantees no field state leaks between tests and is exactly why once-per-class hooks must be `static`.

sections.title: Lifecycle Order
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["@BeforeAll (static)
once per class"] --> B["new test instance"] B --> C["@BeforeEach"] C --> D["@Test method"] D --> E["@AfterEach"] E --> F{"more tests?"} F -->|yes| B F -->|no| G["@AfterAll (static)
once per class"] ```

sections.title: Observing the Order
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming one shared instance.** By default each test gets a new instance; a field mutated in one test is gone in the next.
- **`@BeforeAll` before each test.** It runs once, not per test — that's `@BeforeEach`.
- **Non-static `@BeforeAll`.** Fails to compile/run in the default PER_METHOD mode.
- **Relying on test order.** Methods aren't guaranteed to run top-to-bottom; never depend on it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Order** — `@BeforeAll` → (per test: `@BeforeEach` → `@Test` → `@AfterEach`) → `@AfterAll`.
- **PER_METHOD default** — fresh instance per test enforces isolation.
- **`@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` static** — because no single instance owns them.
- **`@BeforeEach`** is the per-test reset point.
- **No order guarantee** between test methods.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The JUnit 5 lifecycle is a predictable sequence. First, BeforeAll runs once before any test in the class — it's static by default. Then, for each test method, JUnit creates a fresh instance of the test class, runs the BeforeEach methods, runs the actual Test method, and then runs the AfterEach methods. After all the tests have finished, AfterAll runs once. So the shape is BeforeAll once, then a repeating cycle of BeforeEach, test, AfterEach for every method, then AfterAll once.

The detail that ties it all together is the test instance lifecycle. By default it's per-method, which means JUnit creates a brand new object of the test class for every single test. That's deliberate — it guarantees that a field one test sets can't leak into another test, so tests stay independent. And that's exactly why BeforeAll and AfterAll have to be static: since there's no single instance that lives across all the tests, the once-per-class hooks belong at the class level.

The common misconceptions are thinking the same instance is reused across tests, or thinking BeforeAll runs before each test — it doesn't, that's BeforeEach. Another is assuming the test methods run in the order they're written; JUnit doesn't guarantee that, so I never write tests that depend on each other's order. To stand out, I'd connect the per-method default directly to test independence and to the static requirement on BeforeAll, because that shows I understand why the design is the way it is.

question: Can you control the execution order of tests in JUnit 5?
title: JUnit 5 Test Execution Order | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: By default JUnit 5 runs methods in a **deterministic but intentionally non-obvious** order so you don't depend on it. You *can* force an order with **`@TestMethodOrder`** plus **`@Order(n)`** (or alphanumeric/random orderers), but needing a fixed order is usually a **design smell** — well-written tests are independent and pass in any order.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how to set order AND that order-dependent tests are an anti-pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing tests that must run in sequence (e.g. test1 creates data test2 reads), then forcing @Order to mask it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame order control as a rare exception (e.g. documenting a scenario) and emphasize independence

sections.title: Can You Control Test Order?
sections.content: Yes, but you usually shouldn't. By default JUnit 5 uses a **deterministic algorithm that's deliberately not source-order**, precisely to discourage order dependence. When you genuinely need ordering — say a `@Nested` scenario that documents a workflow step by step — annotate the class with **`@TestMethodOrder`** and choose a strategy: `MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation` (with `@Order(n)`), `MethodName`, `DisplayName`, or `Random`. But if a test only passes because another ran first, that's an **independence violation** — fix the test, don't pin the order.

violet|Valid uses|~Rare|documenting a scenario|nested workflow steps|reporting readability

sections.title: Anti-pattern: tests that depend on order
Either: independent tests, or explicit order for a real scenario
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Hidden order dependence.** Relying on a static field set by an earlier test — breaks on parallel runs or reordering.
- **Pinning order to hide a bug.** `@Order` masks the real problem (shared state) instead of fixing it.
- **Assuming source order.** JUnit doesn't run methods top-to-bottom by default.
- **Ordering for speed.** If tests are slow because each recreates data, fix setup, don't sequence them.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Default order** is deterministic but intentionally not source order.
- **`@TestMethodOrder` + `@Order(n)`** force an explicit sequence.
- **Order dependence is a smell** — tests should pass in any order.
- **Valid use** — documenting a workflow scenario, rarely.
- **Fix shared state** instead of pinning order.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Yes, you can control test execution order in JUnit 5, but the more important point is that you usually shouldn't. By default JUnit runs test methods in a deterministic order that's deliberately not the source order. That's an intentional design choice to stop people from accidentally writing tests that depend on running in a particular sequence.

When I really do need an order, I put the TestMethodOrder annotation on the class and pick a strategy. The most common is the order-annotation strategy, where I tag each test with Order and a number. There are also strategies for method name, display name, and even random.

But here's the thing I'd emphasize: if a test only passes because another test ran first — like test one creates a record and test two reads it — that's an independence violation. It's a design smell. It'll break the moment tests run in parallel or get reordered. The fix is to make each test set up its own data, not to pin the order with the Order annotation. Pinning the order just hides the real problem, which is shared mutable state.

There are a few legitimate uses for explicit ordering — for example, a nested test class that documents a checkout workflow step by step, where the order is part of the readability of the report. But that's the exception. To stand out, I'd frame order control as a rare, intentional choice, and stress that well-written tests are independent and pass in any order — that's the Independent in the FIRST principles.

question: How do you use @TempDir in JUnit 5 for file system tests?
title: @TempDir JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@TempDir`** injects a fresh temporary directory (a `Path` or `File`) that JUnit **creates before the test and deletes afterward automatically**, so file-system tests stay clean and isolated. Inject it as a parameter for per-test scope, or as a `static` field for per-class scope. No manual cleanup, no leftover files.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you test file I/O without manual temp-file management or leftover state
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing to a hardcoded path or the project directory and not cleaning up, causing flaky/dirty tests
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note parameter vs static field scope and that @TempDir removes the boilerplate and cleanup risk

sections.title: Temporary Directories, Managed for You
sections.content: **`@TempDir`** tells JUnit to create a unique temporary directory and hand it to your test as a **`Path`** (or `File`), then **delete it automatically** when the test (or class) finishes. This removes the boilerplate of `Files.createTempDirectory` plus try/finally cleanup, and it guarantees each test gets a clean, isolated directory — no leftover files, no cross-test pollution. Inject it as a **method/constructor parameter** for a per-test directory, or as a **`static` field** to share one directory across the class.

sections.content:

blue|Scope|~Parameter vs field|parameter = per test|static field = per class|pick by need
amber|Why|~No manual cleanup|no Files.createTempDirectory|no try/finally|no leftover files
violet|Use for|~File I/O tests|writers, parsers|export/import|config file loading

sections.title: Per-Test and Per-Class Temp Dirs
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Hardcoding a path.** Writing to `/tmp/test.csv` or the project folder leaves files behind and causes flakiness.
- **Manual cleanup.** Reinventing `createTempDirectory` + delete is error-prone; let `@TempDir` do it.
- **Wrong scope.** A parameter `@TempDir` is per test; a `static` field is shared per class — choose deliberately.
- **Assuming a specific location.** The path is system-generated; resolve files relative to the injected dir.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@TempDir`** injects a managed temp directory (`Path`/`File`).
- **Auto create + delete** — no manual cleanup.
- **Parameter** = per-test scope; **`static` field** = per-class scope.
- **Isolation** — each test gets a clean directory.
- **Resolve files** relative to the injected path, never hardcode.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
TempDir is a JUnit 5 feature for testing code that touches the file system. I add the TempDir annotation, and JUnit creates a fresh temporary directory, hands it to me as a Path or a File, and then deletes it automatically when the test finishes. So I get a clean, isolated directory for each test without writing any cleanup code.

The reason it's so useful is that file tests are a classic source of flakiness. If I hardcode a path like slash tmp slash test dot csv, or write into the project directory, I leave files behind, and the next run might see stale data or fail because the file already exists. TempDir removes all of that — there's no Files dot createTempDirectory, no try-finally to delete it, and no leftover files.

There are two ways to inject it, and they differ in scope. If I add it as a method parameter, I get a fresh directory per test, which is the most isolated. If I declare it as a static field, JUnit shares one directory across all the tests in the class, which is handy when several tests build on the same fixture. I just pick based on whether I want isolation or sharing.

In use, I resolve my files relative to the injected directory — for example, tempDir dot resolve orders dot csv — rather than assuming any particular location, because the path is system-generated. The mistakes I'd avoid are hardcoding paths and doing manual cleanup. To stand out, I'd mention the parameter-versus-static-field scoping and that TempDir eliminates both the boilerplate and the cleanup risk.

question: What happens when a @BeforeEach method throws an exception?
title: @BeforeEach Exception Handling JUnit 5 | Java Fresher
direct_answer: If a **`@BeforeEach`** throws, JUnit **aborts that test** (marks it failed) and **skips the `@Test` body** — but it still runs **`@AfterEach`** so cleanup happens. If **`@BeforeAll`** throws, the whole class is aborted and no tests run. This is why setup that can fail (opening resources) belongs in `@BeforeEach`, with cleanup safely in `@AfterEach`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand failure propagation in setup and that @AfterEach still runs after a failed @BeforeEach
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the @Test body still runs, or that @AfterEach is skipped when @BeforeEach fails
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note @AfterEach runs for cleanup even when @BeforeEach failed, and a @BeforeAll failure takes down the class

sections.title: When Setup Fails
sections.content: Setup methods can throw, and JUnit handles it cleanly. If a **`@BeforeEach`** throws, JUnit does **not** run the `@Test` body — the test is marked **failed** with that exception — but it **does** run the `@AfterEach` methods, so any resources already acquired get released. If a **`@BeforeAll`** throws, the failure is more severe: the entire class is aborted and none of its tests run. Understanding this tells you where to put fallible setup: per-test resource acquisition in `@BeforeEach`, with `@AfterEach` guarding cleanup.

sections.title: @BeforeEach Failure Path
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["@BeforeEach runs"] --> B{"throws?"} B -->|no| C["@Test runs"] B -->|yes| D["@Test SKIPPED
test marked failed"] C --> E["@AfterEach runs"] D --> E E --> F["next test"] ```

sections.title: Failure in Setup, Cleanup Still Runs
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking the test still runs.** A failed `@BeforeEach` skips the `@Test` body entirely.
- **Assuming `@AfterEach` is skipped.** It runs even after a failed `@BeforeEach`, so cleanup must be null-safe.
- **Putting fallible setup in `@BeforeAll`.** One throw there aborts every test in the class.
- **Cleanup that assumes setup succeeded.** Guard with null checks since setup may have failed midway.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@BeforeEach` throws** → `@Test` skipped, test marked failed.
- **`@AfterEach` still runs** → cleanup happens regardless.
- **`@BeforeAll` throws** → whole class aborted, no tests run.
- **Make `@AfterEach` null-safe** — setup may have failed partway.
- **Fallible setup** belongs in `@BeforeEach`, not `@BeforeAll`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
If a BeforeEach method throws an exception, JUnit aborts that particular test. It does not run the test body at all, and it marks the test as failed with whatever exception was thrown. But — and this is the important part — it still runs the AfterEach methods. So any resource I already acquired before the exception gets a chance to be released. That's why AfterEach is the safe place for cleanup.

There's a consequence for how I write AfterEach: because it runs even when BeforeEach failed partway through, my cleanup has to be null-safe. If BeforeEach threw before assigning a connection, the field could still be null when AfterEach runs, so I guard with a null check before releasing.

The situation is more severe with BeforeAll. If a BeforeAll method throws, it's a class-level failure — JUnit aborts the entire test class and none of the tests run. That's because BeforeAll is shared setup for everything, so if it can't complete, nothing downstream can proceed.

This actually guides where I put setup. Setup that can realistically fail — like opening a database connection or a file — I prefer to put in BeforeEach, paired with cleanup in AfterEach, so a failure only affects one test rather than wiping out the whole class. The common misconceptions are thinking the test body still runs after a failed BeforeEach, or thinking AfterEach gets skipped. To stand out, I'd point out that AfterEach always runs for cleanup and that a BeforeAll failure takes down the entire class.

question: What is @TestInstance and when would you use PER_CLASS lifecycle?
title: @TestInstance JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@TestInstance`** controls whether JUnit creates one test instance **per method** (the default, `PER_METHOD`) or **one per class** (`PER_CLASS`). With `PER_CLASS`, the same instance is reused across all tests, so `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` can be **non-static** and you can share expensive setup — at the cost of having to reset mutable state yourself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the instance-lifecycle tradeoff and when PER_CLASS is worth the isolation risk
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Switching to PER_CLASS for convenience and then leaking mutable state between tests
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain PER_CLASS enables non-static @BeforeAll and shared setup but you must manage state to keep tests independent

sections.title: One Instance Per Method vs Per Class
sections.content: By default JUnit uses **`PER_METHOD`**: a fresh test instance for every test, which is what keeps tests isolated and forces `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` to be `static`. Adding **`@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`** on the class switches to one shared instance for all tests. The benefits: `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` can be **non-static** (handy when setup needs instance fields), `@MethodSource` factories can be non-static, and you can build an expensive resource once and share it. The cost: state now persists across tests, so you must reset mutable fields in `@BeforeEach` to preserve independence.

sections.title: PER_METHOD vs PER_CLASS
sections.content:
emerald|PER_METHOD (default)|~Fresh instance per test|maximum isolation|@BeforeAll must be static|no state leaks
blue|PER_CLASS|~One instance per class|@BeforeAll can be non-static|non-static @MethodSource|share expensive setup
amber|The tradeoff|~Convenience vs safety|state persists across tests|reset in @BeforeEach|you own isolation
violet|Use PER_CLASS when|~Costly shared setup|big in-memory fixture|stateful @MethodSource|but be disciplined

sections.title: PER_METHOD: @BeforeAll must be static
PER_CLASS: non-static @BeforeAll + shared setup
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Leaking state in PER_CLASS.** A field mutated by one test affects the next; reset it in `@BeforeEach`.
- **Using PER_CLASS just to avoid `static`.** That convenience can silently introduce order-dependence.
- **Forgetting it's opt-in.** PER_METHOD is the default; you must annotate the class for PER_CLASS.
- **Assuming Spring tests need it.** Spring reuses the *context*, not the test instance — separate concern.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`PER_METHOD`** (default) — fresh instance per test, maximum isolation.
- **`PER_CLASS`** — one shared instance; `@BeforeAll` can be non-static.
- **Benefit** — share expensive setup, non-static `@MethodSource`.
- **Cost** — state persists; reset mutable fields in `@BeforeEach`.
- **Opt-in** via `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
TestInstance controls how many instances of the test class JUnit creates. The default is per-method, which means a fresh instance for every test. That's what gives you isolation, and it's the reason BeforeAll and AfterAll have to be static — there's no single instance that lives across all the tests.

If I put TestInstance with the per-class lifecycle on the class, JUnit creates just one instance and reuses it for every test. That unlocks a few conveniences. BeforeAll and AfterAll can now be non-static, which is helpful when my once-per-class setup needs to touch instance fields. MethodSource factory methods can also be non-static. And I can build an expensive resource once and share it across all the tests in the class.

The catch is that state now persists between tests, because they share the instance. So if one test mutates a field, the next test sees it. That undermines independence, so the discipline is to reset any mutable state in BeforeEach. In other words, per-class hands me the isolation responsibility that per-method handled automatically.

So I'd use per-class when there's genuinely expensive shared setup or I need a stateful MethodSource, but I'd be careful to reset state. The mistake I'd warn against is reaching for per-class just to avoid writing static, because that can quietly introduce order-dependent tests. One clarification I'd add to stand out: Spring reuses the application context across tests for speed, but that's a different mechanism from the JUnit test instance lifecycle.
